title: Nine people, one hour
setting: A project meeting with more people in it than decisions to make.

lines.t: Let's kick off. Two minutes of small talk and then we get down to business.
That's the shortest break the ice I've ever been given.
Nine people, one hour. I'd rather cut to the chase.
Fine. Are we going over the whole plan or just the budget?
The budget. On everything else we're already on the same page.
Then somebody should bring up the elephant in the room. We're two people short.
Say it properly, so it goes in the notes.
We planned this for six people and four are available. In a nutshell, the date moves or the scope does.
Does anyone want to weigh in?
Mira has been on the fence since Monday. Mira, speak up.
She just did, in chat. She and Deyan don't see eye to eye on the order of the work.
Then those two take it offline and come back with one answer on Thursday.
We haven't touched on the budget for the extra week.
Off the top of my head, eleven thousand. Don't quote me on that.
Run the real figure by Radost before Thursday.
I'll touch base with her tomorrow and circle back to the group on Friday.
Do we need a session to brainstorm alternatives?
Not a whole session. I'll bounce a few ideas off Kiril over coffee and bring you two options.
And if the supplier is late again?
We play it by ear. Long story short, the big picture hasn't changed: we ship in April, or we ship badly.
Anybody want to chime in before I wrap up?
Just read back the action items. The takeaways can go in the email, and the bottom line is Thursday.

title: The deadline moved
setting: Ivan tells his colleague Dana the client meeting is two days earlier.

lines.t: Dana, quick heads up. The client moved the meeting to Wednesday.
Wednesday? That's two days earlier. Where are we with the proposal?
About half done. I'd rather cut the scope than send something weak.
Agreed. Which sections actually matter to them?
That's what I asked them. They said pricing, timeline and the team.
So the market analysis can go. That saves you a day.
Can I run the new structure by you before I write it?
Send it over. I have the bandwidth this afternoon.
Thanks. I'll keep you posted if anything changes.
Do that. And let's not touch it after six, it's already been a long week.

title: Reply all
setting: Somebody has sent a client thread more than they meant to.

lines.t: Quick heads up. I hit reply all.
On the client thread?
On the client thread. With a typo in the first line.
Did anyone get back to you?
Their project manager, in four minutes, being very kind about it.
Then it's survivable. Did you cc anyone internally?
I looped Radost in, because she signs off on anything they see.
Good. Keep me posted if they raise it again, and keep Radost in the loop.
Should I reach out and apologise properly?
One line, to him only. Then proofread the next one before it goes.
I'll double-check everything for a month.
You'll double-check for a week and then forget, like the rest of us. Follow up on the actual question they asked, because that's still unanswered, and follow through on the date you give them.

title: Six o'clock
setting: A manager and a team lead talk about two people on the way out of the door.

lines.t: It's six. Let's call it a day.
One thing first. Nadya is ready to take the lead on the Varna account.
She's been here four months.
She learned the ropes faster than anyone I've had, and she got up to speed on the contracts in a fortnight.
And Boyan?
He dropped the ball twice this month. Both times on something he'd promised.
Is he pulling his weight otherwise?
He's a team player and he goes the extra mile whenever anyone asks. He can't say no, so he agrees to everything and finishes half.
Then teach him to say no before you ask him to step up on anything else.
Tomorrow. Now it really is six.

title: Back to the drawing board
setting: Six weeks of effort and the numbers have not moved.

lines.t: Six weeks, and the numbers haven't moved.
Nothing we tried moved the needle?
One thing. The rest was trial and error, mostly error.
Then it's back to the drawing board on the big idea. What's the quick win?
Answering the phone before five rings. Low-hanging fruit, and a no-brainer.
Do that on Monday and get the ball rolling while we figure out the rest.
We still have to deal with the booking system.
Can you sort it out, or do we need the supplier?
There's a workaround. It's ugly and it works.
Use it while we nail down a real answer. What's plan B if the supplier says no?
We come up with something ourselves, which costs three weeks.
Then iron out the details this week. My rule of thumb is never to cut corners on the part customers touch.
Agreed. I'll send you the game plan tonight, and then the ball is in your court on the budget.

title: Too much on my plate
setting: A manager asks someone to take on another project.

lines.t: Elena, could you take on the onboarding project as well?
I'd like to, but I have too much on my plate this month.
What's taking most of your time?
The two client reports and covering for Stefan while he's away.
Right. When does Stefan get back?
The fifteenth. After that I'd have the bandwidth.
Let's pencil it in for the sixteenth, then.
That works. Can we go over the scope before it starts?
Of course. I'll set up a short call for Friday.
Perfect. Then I can hit the ground running.

title: Crunch time
setting: A manager asks for an honest answer about what will actually be finished.

lines.t: Where are we? Honestly.
Two things on track, one running behind, one up in the air.
Which one is behind schedule?
The catalogue. I've been putting it off because it's time-consuming and nobody chases it.
And the one up in the air?
The Plovdiv visit. I'd pencil it in for the 14th and call it off on Friday if the numbers don't arrive.
Fine. What's on your plate this week?
Too much. I'm filling in for Kiril, and I took on the supplier forms on short notice.
Do you have the bandwidth for the catalogue as well?
No. Something gets put on hold, or somebody takes it over.
Then hand the forms over to Nadya. She can fill them out and set up the meeting.
That helps. If I stop juggling three things I'll stop getting sidetracked.
Put together a list of what's in the pipeline and keep track of the dates in one place. And make time for the catalogue on Tuesday, before anything else.
Then if we run out of time in March it's crunch time we saw coming. I've had enough of finishing at the last minute, down to the wire, every quarter.
